title: Sort machined blocks with a go/no-go gap gauge
instruction: Check each of the seven aluminium blocks with the gauge. A block that drops into the green GO gap but not into the red NO-GO gap is in tolerance: put it in the green tray. Put every other block in the red tray.
context: Checking parts against fixed-limit gauges is routine work for machinists and quality inspectors, and passing an out-of-tolerance block (an escape) is the costly mistake. Unlike picking the one pin that fits a hole, every block in a batch must be classified against two limits.
setup: Station table. Coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline between them, z up from the table top; the arm bases are at y = +0.305 (left) and y = -0.305 (right). Loose: seven bare aluminium blocks, each 50 mm long (along x) by 20 mm tall, lying flat, their widths (along y) differing; specified width 30.0 +- 3.0 mm. Left row, y = +0.30: block 1, 30.5 mm wide, at x 0.16; block 2, 34.5 mm, x 0.25; block 3, 28.5 mm, x 0.34; block 4, 25.5 mm, x 0.43. Right row, y = -0.30: block 5, 35.0 mm, x 0.16; block 6, 29.5 mm, x 0.25; block 7, 25.0 mm, x 0.34. Each weighs 2.7 g per mm of width (68 to 95 g). Their numbers are written on their undersides, out of the cameras' view. Fixed, screwed down: the gauge, centred at (0.13, 0): a dark grey steel base 100 x 160 x 10 mm (x, y, z) with two pairs of anvils on top, each anvil 10 x 20 x 15 mm. The green pair forms the GO gap, 33.0 mm between inner faces, centred at y = +0.04; the red pair forms the NO-GO gap, 27.0 mm, centred at y = -0.04. Both gaps run along x, so a block lying along x drops into a gap when it is narrower, onto the base 15 mm below the anvil tops. Two open trays across the midline, each 80 x 220 mm inside, 5 mm floor, 6 mm walls standing 25 mm above the table: the red reject tray centred at x 0.24 and the green pass tray centred at x 0.35. Real-world build: blocks are 6061 bar stock milled to width (+-0.05 mm) and numbered underneath; the gauge base, anvils and trays are printed PLA or machined aluminium, the anvils set to the gap widths with a caliper, screwed or glued down.
scoring: End state, read after the arms stop and open, from a top photo and a tape. Blocks 1, 3 and 6 are in tolerance; 2, 4, 5 and 7 are not. A block is in a tray when its centre is over the tray's inside (within 40 mm of the tray's centre along x and 110 mm along y), its lowest point is no more than 50 mm above the table (resting on the floor or on one layer of blocks), and it is still (under 1 cm/s). Score = (C - 2F - 2E) / 7, at least 0, where C counts blocks in the right tray, F counts in-tolerance blocks in the red tray (false rejects) and E counts out-of-tolerance blocks in the green tray (escapes); if E is 1 or more, the score is at most 0.25. A block anywhere else (on the table, in or on the gauge, on a rim, held, off the table) counts for nothing. Full score (1.0) is all seven blocks in the right trays; the trial ends early once that holds for 1 s. The gauge and trays are fixed; nothing done to them earns or loses credit. Putting every block in the red tray, or every block in the green tray, scores 0; sorting them at random scores about 0.052 on average.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Return each block, by the number on its underside, to its starting place, lying along x.
fidelity: Approximate. Blocks, gauge and trays are rigid boxes with one shared rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than aluminium on steel. The tolerance is scaled up: real gap gauges work to hundredths of a millimetre, here every block clears or misses each gap by at least 1.5 mm in width (0.75 mm a side), and every in-tolerance block clears the GO gap by at least 2.0 mm (1.0 mm a side), so the simulated contacts resolve it. The anvils have square edges with no lead-in chamfer, so a block that is in tolerance but held more than about 7 degrees off the gap's axis can catch on the anvils, as with a real gauge. Masses follow aluminium's density.
